title_eng: Orthopedic surgeon level joint angle assessment with artificial intelligence based on photography: a pilot study
abstract:
Accurate assessment of shoulder range of motion (ROM) is crucial for evaluating patient progress. Traditional manual 
goniometry often lacks precision and is subject to inter-observer variability, especially in measuring shoulder internal rota -
tion (IR). This study introduces an artificial intelligence (AI)-based approach that uses clinical photography to improve the 
accuracy of ROM quantification. We analyzed a total of 150 clinical photographs, including 100 shoulder and 50 elbow 
images, taken between January and April 2022. An MMPose model with an HR-NET backbone architecture, pre-trained 
on the COCO-WholeBody dataset, was used to detect 17 anatomical landmarks. A random forest classifier (PoseRF) then 
categorized poses, and ROM angles were calculated. Concurrently, two clinicians independently measured shoulder IR at 
the vertebral level, and inter-observer agreement was evaluated. Linear regression analyses were conducted to correlate 
the AI-derived measurements with the clinicians’ assessments. The AI-based algorithm accurately detected anatomical 
landmarks in 96% of shoulder and 100% of elbow images. Pose detection achieved 95% accuracy overall, with 100% 
accuracy for specific shoulder (abduction, flexion, external rotation) and elbow (flexion, extension) poses. Intraclass corre -
lation coefficients (ICCs) between the AI algorithm and human observers ranged from 0.965 to 0.997, indicating excellent 
inter-observer reliability. Kruskal-Wallis test showed no statistically significant differences in ROM measurements among 
the AI algorithm and two human observers across all joint angles ( p > 0.05). The AI-based algorithm demonstrated per -
formance comparable to that of human observers in quantifying shoulder and elbow ROM from clinical photographs. For 
shoulder internal rotation, the AI approach showed potential for improved consistency compared to traditional methods.

1 Introduction
The most traditional and accurate way to measure range of 
motion (ROM) is with a goniometer [ 1]. However, some 
angles, such as internal rotation (IR) of the shoulder, are 
impossible to measure with a goniometer [ 2] It can also be 
time-consuming and laborious for a physician to measure 
ROM manually.
Measuring the IR of the shoulder joint is challeng -
ing because the hand is obscured by the torso. Therefore, 
numerous researchers have indirectly measured the position 
of the thumb at the vertebral level [ 2–5]. However, there 
have been reports of poor inter-observer agreement [6]. 
Numerous studies have explored automated approaches 
for measuring shoulder and elbow angles. Werner et al. 
used a smartphone clinometer to measure shoulder ROM 
and showed good agreement; however, it is still time-con -
suming and requires the help of another physician to record 
the photo as a medical record [7]. Furthermore, an artificial 
intelligence (AI)-based algorithm was developed. Fan et al. 
showed high inter-observer agreement using a pose tracking 
technique with a commercial digital camera and the Open -
pose library [8]. However, this technique is difficult to use 
in practice because it requires a large space and multiple 
cameras. Wang et al. compared two AI algorithms, Opti-
Track and BlazePose [ 9], and showed high inter-observer 
agreement; however, this method is video-based, making it 
difficult to measure the maximum ROM angle.
In numerous medical centers, physicians routinely cap -
ture clinical photographs to document ROM for medical 
records. However, the reliability and accuracy of manual 
ROM measurements using these photographs have not 
been extensively investigated. The primary objective of this 
study is to evaluate the inter-observer reliability between 
an AI algorithm, specifically the MMPose model [ 10], and 
human observers in measuring shoulder and elbow ROM 
using clinical photographs. Additionally, we aim to assess 
the reliability of human measurements of shoulder IR using 
these images. We hypothesize that AI algorithms can be eas-
ily applied to clinical photographs and will demonstrate reli-
able results, potentially offering advantages over traditional 
manual assessments in terms of consistency and accuracy.
2 Materials and methods
2.1 Retrospective study
This retrospective study was conducted in accordance with 
the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and current 
scientific guidelines. The research protocol was approved 
by the Institutional Review Board of Asan Medical 
Center (S2023-0927-0001), which waived the requirement 
for informed consent due to the retrospective nature of the 
study and the de-identified characteristics of the dataset, as 
per the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act 
privacy rule.
2.2 Dataset
All 50 consecutive shoulder clinical photographs and 25 
elbow clinical photographs taken between January and 
April 2022 at our institution were utilized. The photos were 
of patients hospitalized for surgery for elbow and shoulder 
conditions. The shoulder group consisted of 50 patients 
(mean age 64.2 ± 8.5 years; 16 males, 34 females), while 
the elbow group comprised 25 patients (mean age 57.3 ± 8.5 
years; 19 males, 6 females). Using these photographs, we 
measured shoulder bilateral abduction, unilateral forward 
flexion (FF) on the affected side, bilateral IR, and bilateral 
external rotation (ER). For the elbow, we measured unilat -
eral flexion and extension. The measurements taken by the 
shoulder and elbow fellow (observer 1) were considered the 
ground truth values.
The dataset underwent random stratification, with 50% 
allocated for model training and 50% for testing purposes. 
Furthermore, 20% of the training data was reserved for vali-
dation. This stratification resulted in the following distribu-
tion: 40 shoulder and 20 elbow measurements for training, 
10 shoulder and 5 elbow measurements for validation, and 
50 shoulder and 25 elbow measurements for testing.
2.3 Definition of landmarks and measuring real 
angles
First, two clinicians, a shoulder and elbow fellow (observer 
1) and an orthopedic resident (observer 2), each looked at 
the photos and noted the center of rotation of the shoul -
der, elbow, and wrist using the Visual Geometry Group 
(VGG) image annotator [11]. The clinical photographs were 
assumed to be perpendicular to the ground and the angle 
was measured (Fig. 1). Using the MMPose library, the AI 
algorithm took the same photo as input and extracted the 
center of the joint as a landmark [10]. 
Abduction: Measured from the front view, using the 
angle between the vertical axis and the line connecting the 
shoulder and elbow landmarks. Shoulder FF: Measured 
from the side view, calculating the angle between the verti-
cal axis and the line from shoulder to elbow landmarks. ER: 
Measured from the front view as the angle between the fore-
arm (elbow to wrist landmarks) and the vertical axis passing 
through the elbow. IR: Measured in two ways: (a) From the 
back view, calculating the angle between the forearm and 
the vertical axis passing through the elbow. (b) By clinicians

2.4 Model pipeline
We have developed a three-stage pipeline that integrates 
advanced computer vision techniques with AI models for 
AI-assisted assessment of shoulder and elbow ROM assess-
ment using clinical photography. This approach ensures pre-
cise and reliable ROM measurement (Fig. 2).

In the second stage, we developed PoseRF, a random 
forest model designed for pose detection based on detected 
landmarks. MMPose alone does not classify specific poses 
such as abduction or FF. PoseRF categorizes poses based 
on landmark coordinates extracted by MMPose. This model 
leverages the discriminative power of the random forest 
algorithm to classify captured poses into distinct classes 
using the 17 landmark coordinates as input features. PoseRF 
was trained on a dataset comprising 50 shoulder and 25 
elbow images, each annotated with the 17 landmark points. 
To enhance robustness and generalizability, we employed 
data augmentation techniques including translation, rota -
tion (within 10 degrees), and random jittering [ 14]. These 
augmentations increased dataset diversity, enabling PoseRF 
to achieve high accuracy in pose detection. Hyperparameter 
optimization using grid search in Scikit-Learn selected 100 
trees with maximum depth set to None. Key hyperparam -
eters included minimum samples required to split a node 
(10), minimum samples required at a leaf node (2), and 
‘entropy’ as the split quality criterion. Maximum features 
for splitting were set to automatic mode, enhancing random-
ness and reducing tree correlation, resulting in a robust pose 
detection model.
In the first stage of the pipeline, we utilize the MMPose 
model (v1.2) to detect anatomical landmarks of human 
across various poses. MMPose, built on an HRNet-w48 
backbone pretrained on the COCO-WholeBody dataset 
[13], efficiently detects humans and then extracts X and Y 
coordinates of 17 key anatomical landmarks from single 
images. These landmarks include left and right shoulders, 
elbows, wrists, as well as facial features like nose and eyes. 
This capability addresses the complexity of clinical photo -
graphs where pose order may vary or additional/missing 
poses can occur. Prior to the input of data into MMPose, 
standard preprocessing protocols were rigorously followed, 
including normalization according to ImageNet standards. 
Specifically, the data were normalized using mean values 
of [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and standard deviations of [0.229, 
0.224, 0.225] across the RGB channels, thereby ensuring
